extracted.intended_audience: readers of The Spectator; literate public interested in manners, wit, satire, and social criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and normative observations for composing and understanding satirical/moral essays on wit, social behaviour, marriage, clubs, and superstition in the style of The Spectator. Covers what counts as good or vicious forms of wit and social conduct and gives examples and anti-patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Biter / Biting (a way of wit)
rubrics_metrics.description: This way of Wit is called 'Biting'... A Biter is one who thinks you a Fool, because you do not think him a Knave.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains the metaphor (foxes devouring harmless animals) and traces the phrase from sharpers to shallow fops; describes how a 'Biter' depends on deceit, making the audience appear credulous. Examples & anti-patterns: a person tells a serious-sounding falsehood and cries 'Bite' when the listener takes it seriously; using particulars to give false authority to a jest (e.g. the Yorkshire/apoplexy story, and the surgeon/condemned-man carcass story where the rogue takes the money then cries 'Bite, I am to be hang'd in Chains'). Tone: portrayed as silly, pernicious, and frivolous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid deceptive 'bite' jokes that make the audience the butt
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'Bite' is an exploit where the speaker over-reaches an innocent person and then triumphs that he has deceiv'd them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characterises biting as relying on deceit rather than wit; condemned as discouraging modesty and honest arts. The essay counsels against celebrating or imitating such behaviour — it is a knavish dependence on deceit for advantage in wit or interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skepticism toward dream-interpretation (Oneirocritick)
rubrics_metrics.description: Dreams are 'uncertain, shadowy, and chimerical' and the many arts of prediction (lines of the hand, faces, stars, entrails) are groundless; multitudes remain slaves to such follies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parodic 'Oneirocritick' letter exposes the charlatan: invented credentials (second-sighted great-uncle), improbable physical signs (four fingers and two thumbs), exotic origin stories (born on longest night), lodging in Moorfields/Bedlam, tiered fees (free to poor in exchange for advertising, charges for lovers/gentlewomen), and gimmicks such as interpreting by seeing a person's water. Use of these features signals a fraudulent interpreter; the essay recommends rooting out popular errors and not laying stress on dream-omens in ordinary life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not let fear of the future or superstition govern conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Men suffer more from apprehension and groundless presages than from real evils; many predictions are trivial and ridiculous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lists varieties of divination and portents (days, numbers, voices, figures, straws, rusty iron) as examples of superstitious interpretation to be rejected. The normative point: favour reason and reject arts of prediction that have no reliable basis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condemnation of 'Party-lying' and standards for truthfulness
rubrics_metrics.description: Party-lying — propagating a system of lies for factional ends — is a predominant and detestable vice; truth is essential as virtue and part of the divine nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyzes three motives people give for party-lies and refutes them: (1) that guilt is diminished by numbers (counter: guilt is not divided but multiplied), (2) that shame is annihilated in multitudes (counter: it makes one an infamous hypocrite who values appearance over reality), (3) that lies may serve a good cause (counter: ends do not justify falsehood). Upholds the principle that one should not tell lies for temporal reward or factional advantage (quoting the extreme formulation: 'He would not tell a Lie, tho' he were sure to gain Heaven by it').

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth and intellectual discipline as moral goods
rubrics_metrics.description: Truth is likened to the body of the Supreme Being and is as necessary as virtue to qualify the soul; mathematical demonstration and sciences are purgatives of the soul to cleanse it from error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implied standard for writers/speakers: cultivate and communicate truth; value intellectual disciplines that curb error; avoid rhetorical tricks that favour appearance over truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep love alive after marriage by effort and good sense
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not sufficient that humours be alike; to preserve love there must be an earnest endeavour to please on both sides and 'superior good Sense on the part of Man.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defines 'Man of Sense' as one 'acquainted with Business and Letters.' Encourages continual attentions that make conversation new and agreeable over decades; criticises complacency after 'catching' a spouse. The standard for conduct: active cultivation of affection through civility, intellectual stimulation, and refined behaviour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid too-great familiarity and lapses in decency in marriage
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing has more contributed to banish love from a married state than too great a Familiarity, and laying aside the common Rules of Decency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warns that familiarity breeds contempt and kills tenderness; cites examples (women dressing casually before husbands) as gross faults that erode affection. Norm: maintain decorum and small courtesies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Neatness and tasteful dress preserve a spouse's esteem
rubrics_metrics.description: Neglect of neatness and dress are faults that make a wife lose her husband's heart; Beaus who stop 'baiting' after marriage exemplify this mistake.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use contrasts: Erastus (cultivated, shows wife new worlds, polite, complaisant) vs Tom Tawdry (vain dress, idle life, despised). The advice: continue to 'dress' your relationship—attention to appearance and tasteful behaviour keeps desire and esteem alive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain occupations and occasional absences to preserve interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Some small engagement in business not only sets a man's talents in a fair light but gives occasions for little absences which preserve desire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Norm for married men: have pursuits outside domestic life to create interest and prevent the staleness of constant availability; it provides material for conversation and preserves the spouse's esteem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use complaisance and discreet flattery to raise a partner's esteem
rubrics_metrics.description: By artful complaisance a man can make his wife discover good qualities in herself and attribute ideas to her own judgment, thereby increasing her fondness and self-satisfaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tactic illustrated: praise a purchase or opinion as her judgment, give remote hints that lead her to proposals, then receive them as her discovery. Ethical limit implicit: this is 'artful' but meant to cultivate mutual pleasure rather than deceive maliciously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Politeness toward female guests: do not contradict or insult
rubrics_metrics.description: Guests (especially women) should be treated with gentleness and not contradicted or accused of lying; calling a woman 'a liar' or contradicting her on all occasions is rude and injurious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Letter complains of a gentleman who contradicts a female guest constantly and even told her she lied; prescriptive standard: treat women 'as gently as their Sisters' and avoid gratuitous contradictions—this is a matter of civility and good breeding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Norms for club/meeting governance (against 'Dionysius' tyranny)
rubrics_metrics.description: An officer (proveditor) in a club should undertake tasks to serve the public felicity, recommend but not impose, and allow disputable choices; assuming absolute and unalterable edicts is tyrannical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes abuses: usurping authority (issuing edicts as unalterable as Medes and Persians), interrupting or promoting conversation by personal humour, dictating where and how the company shall meet, and using office to parade authority. Recommended remedy: collective resistance and removal of such a tyrant (satirically proposed 'dethroning' by satirical dinner), and re-establishing moderate, consultative governance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frugality and regularity as marks of thrift and civic prosperity
rubrics_metrics.description: The thriving frugal man shows it in every part of his expense, dress, servants, and house; simplicity of manners is the true source of wealth and prosperity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses the neglected state of the Royal-Exchange and its walkways as a civic symptom: if public commercial spaces are overrun by beggars and trivial sellers, the city's antient economy and regularity are declining. Norm for citizens: preserve public order and the dignity of commercial assemblies; personal frugality manifests in orderly dress and domestic economy.
